content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.7. The evidence leans that way but isn't conclusive, because the test results were very noisy.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M3. Then I tested new tasks with 0, 1 or 3 rules the learner hadn't seen. For the 1-new-rule case, I picked one task that shares two rules with a trained task and one that shares at most one rule with any trained task.

| Test tasks | New rules | Samples | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M3, L2-S1-M1, L1-S1-M3 | 0 | 24 | ≈28.5 |
| L1-S1-M4 (shares two rules with L1-S1-M1) | 1 | 12 | 22.4 |
| L3-S2-M1 (shares at most one rule with any trained task) | 1 | 12 | 30.1 |
| L4-S4-M4, L3-S3-M2 | 3 | 10 | ≈47 |

**Why holistic:**
- **New rules didn't add cost one by one.** Part-based predicts that a task with 1 new rule takes longer than one with 0 new rules. The 1-new-rule tasks were no slower than the 0-new ones.
- **Similarity predicted cost better.** The 1-new-rule task most similar to a trained task was the fastest task tested. The less similar 1-new-rule task was slower, even though both have exactly one new rule.

**Caveats:**
- Repeated tests of the same task varied a lot, roughly ±15–20 examples, so the gaps between the 0-new and 1-new groups are close to the noise level.
- The one clear effect is that tasks with 3 new rules took longer. Both hypotheses predict that, so it doesn't help tell them apart.

I used the full budget of 60 before submitting.
